title: Vayera: visiting the sick (Genesis 18:1)
hook: God appears to Abraham as he heals; the rabbis learn that God visits the sick (Sotah 14a)
tomorrow: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, new names: Abram became Abraham, Sarai became Sarah, and the covenant of circumcision began. Your line was a name can grow. Today, a new portion: Vayera.

When someone's sick, it can be hard to know what to do. What do you say? Will a visit intrude? Maybe they want rest. So a text goes out instead: a heart emoji, get well soon. The fourth portion of the Torah opens with a single quiet verse: God appears to Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day. It doesn't say why. But the rabbis looked at where this verse sits, right after Abraham's circumcision, and drew a conclusion that became a whole Jewish practice.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY?` → `A TEXT, A HEART EMOJI.` → `GOD APPEARS AT THE TENT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Vayera, and he appeared, from its first verse: "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." Why does God appear? No message, no command. Just presence. The rabbis noticed that the verse right before tells of Abraham's circumcision, at ninety-nine. So Abraham is recovering, sore, sitting in the shade. The Talmud says God came to visit the sick, to ask after his welfare. Then it builds a whole teaching on it. The Torah says to walk after the LORD your God. How can a person walk after God? By copying God's ways. God clothed the naked, Adam and Eve; so you clothe the naked. God visited the sick, Abraham; so you visit the sick. God comforted mourners, Isaac after his father died; so you comfort mourners. God buried the dead, Moses; so you bury the dead. The Hebrew for visiting the sick is bikur cholim: bikur, a visit, and cholim, the sick. It's a mitzvah, a commandment, and some Jewish communities have a bikur cholim group whose whole job is to show up. The Talmud even says a visitor takes away a small part of the illness, one sixtieth. It's not medicine. It's company. The rabbis give the visitor practical advice too: don't sit up high over the sick person; sit at their level. And they expect a visitor to ask for mercy for the one who is sick. Just by showing up, the rabbis say, a visitor does what God did at a tent door on a hot day.
screen: `AND THE LORD APPEARED UNTO HIM.` · `AFTER THE CIRCUMCISION, HEALING.` · `WALK AFTER GOD: CLOTHE, VISIT, COMFORT.` · `ONE SIXTIETH OF THE ILLNESS.` · then, large: `VISIT THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who's sick, hurting or recovering, near or far, and picture yourself sitting beside them, at their level, not standing over them. You don't need to say anything clever; just be there. If you pray, ask for their healing; if you don't, hold them in mind with warmth.
Bikur cholim. Visiting the sick: a Jewish commandment learned from God, who appeared to Abraham as he healed.
Your line: visit the sick. Not a text: your voice, or your face. Day one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Visiting the sick is a mitzvah in Jewish law; some synagogues have bikur cholim volunteers who visit hospitals and homes, and the Mi Sheberach prayer for healing is said during the Torah reading.

fork.setup: a friend is recovering from surgery. you're not sure they want company. what does the Jewish teaching suggest?
options: send a text and stay away.
visit, briefly, and sit at their level.
fork.reveal: show up, and sit at their level, not over them. that's bikur cholim, and it's what God did at the tent door.

trapdoor: what you thought: God came to Abraham to deliver a message.
what it means: God simply appears to Abraham while he heals, and the rabbis learn that visiting the sick is walking in God's ways.
what a scholar hears: Sotah 14a (Rabbi Chama bar Chanina on Deuteronomy 13:5); Bava Metzia 86b (third day after the circumcision); Nedarim 39b–40a (one sixtieth; guidance for visitors).

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 18:1 ('terebinths of Mamre').
Sotah 14a: the four examples (clothing Adam and Eve, visiting Abraham, comforting Isaac, burying Moses) and the verse 'walk after the LORD your God' (Deuteronomy 13:5 in JPS numbering). Confirm.
Nedarim 39b (one sixtieth) and the guidance on timing and sitting at the patient's level (Nedarim 40a; Shabbat 12b; later codes). Confirm the combination.
'Pray for them, if you pray': invitational; confirm.
The three visitors (18:2–8) are not retold here; day 177 mentions them only as the setup for Sodom.
